Celibacy is the deliberate choice to abstain from sexual activity and, in many cases, from marriage — and to maintain that choice as a long-term or even lifelong commitment.

When someone is "in a state of celibacy," it simply means they have made a conscious decision to not engage in sexual relations, and they are actively living by that decision.

Think of it this way. Most people, at some point in their lives, happen to not be in a sexual relationship. That alone does not make them celibate. What makes someone truly celibate is the deliberate, committed decision to avoid sexual activity — it is an intentional, sustained choice, not just a circumstance.

Celibacy is not something that happens to you. It is something you choose and commit to.

The word carries two closely related but slightly distinct ideas:

1. Abstaining from sex
This is the most widely understood meaning today. A celibate person does not engage in sexual activity — not with a partner, not casually, not at all.

2. Abstaining from marriage
In its fuller, more traditional sense, celibacy also means choosing not to marry. This is because, historically and in many religious traditions, marriage and sexual relations were inseparable. To commit to one was to commit to the other.

In modern everyday usage, when people say someone is "celibate," they usually mean the person is not having sex — with or without a stance on marriage.

There are two broad motivations:

Religious or spiritual reasons — This is the most historically prominent reason. Many religions call upon certain members to live celibately so they can dedicate themselves fully to God, spiritual practice, or service to others. The idea is that sexual and romantic relationships demand emotional energy, time, and attachment — and by removing those, a person can channel everything into their faith or spiritual path.

  • Catholic priests and nuns take a vow of celibacy as part of their commitment to the Church.
  • Buddhist monks and nuns in many traditions practice celibacy as part of their monastic vows.
  • Certain Hindu spiritual seekers (called sannyasis or brahmacharis) practice celibacy as a form of spiritual discipline.

Personal, philosophical, or practical reasons — Not everyone who chooses celibacy does so for religion. Some people choose it because:

  • They want to focus on personal goals, career, or self-development without the distraction or emotional complexity of sexual relationships.
  • They have experienced past trauma and need time and space to heal.
  • They hold personal values that lead them to reserve sex for a specific kind of committed relationship (like marriage), and they are waiting for that.
  • They simply feel no strong desire for sexual activity and find celibacy natural and comfortable for them.

Celibacy can be:

  • Permanent — A lifelong commitment, typically seen in religious figures like priests or monks who have taken formal vows.
  • Long-term — A person may commit to celibacy for an extended phase of their life — perhaps years — for personal or spiritual growth, without necessarily committing to it forever.
  • Temporary — Some people practice celibacy for a defined period, like during a time of healing, reflection, or waiting for marriage.

The word "celibacy" does not tell you how long someone has committed to it — that depends on the person and their specific choice.
Celibacy vs. Three Words People Confuse It With

These words are related but not the same, and confusing them is very common.

Celibacy vs. Abstinence
Abstinence means refraining from something — in this context, refraining from sex. The difference is mostly one of scope and commitment. Abstinence can be short-term, situational, or limited to specific acts. Celibacy implies a broader, more defined, and more committed way of life. All celibate people are abstinent, but not everyone who is abstinent is celibate.

Celibacy vs. Chastity
Chastity is about moral and ethical purity in matters of sexuality, in accordance with one's values or beliefs. A married person can absolutely be chaste — it simply means they are faithful and sexually ethical within their relationship. Celibacy, on the other hand, means no sexual relationship at all. So chastity is a moral standard that can apply within or outside of relationships, while celibacy is a life choice to not have sexual relations at all.

Celibacy vs. Asexuality
Asexuality is a sexual orientation — it means a person experiences little to no sexual attraction toward others. It is about how someone feels. Celibacy is about what someone does (or chooses not to do). An asexual person may naturally have little interest in sex, but they are not automatically celibate because of it. Conversely, a celibate person may experience sexual attraction — they simply choose not to act on it.

This is an important distinction.

Voluntary celibacy is what the word truly and traditionally refers to — a free, intentional decision made by the person themselves.

Involuntary celibacy describes a situation where someone is not having sex not because they chose it, but because they lack the opportunity or partner. This is a different experience entirely, and the word "celibacy" in its proper sense does not apply here — though the phrase "involuntary celibacy" (sometimes shortened to "incel") has entered popular vocabulary to describe this situation.

True celibacy is always a choice.

Celibacy is the deliberate, committed choice to abstain from sexual activity — and often from marriage — either for religious, spiritual, or personal reasons. It is a sustained, intentional way of living, not merely the temporary absence of a sexual relationship.
